explanation: The subject of the verb is "the triangle," which is singular, so the verb must be singular: "is." The phrase "representing the mountain itself" just describes the triangle. "Are," "have been," and "were" are all plural forms, and the text describes her paintings in a general, ongoing way, so present-tense "is" fits.

"While filming a boxing match for the movie Body and Soul (1947)" is an introductory phrase, and a comma should separate it from the main clause "Howe had a handheld camera operator wear roller skates." Adding "and" (choices A and C) wrongly joins a phrase to a clause as if they were two equal clauses, and leaving out punctuation (D) runs the introductory phrase into the main clause.

"The Puerto Rican municipality of Aibonito is well known for its lush greenery" and "this distinction has earned it the fitting nickname..." are both independent clauses, and a semicolon correctly joins them. A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation or just "and" without a comma creates a run-on.

Misaka's military service and championships happened before another past event—joining the Knicks in 1947. An action completed before another past action calls for the past perfect, "had already served." Simple past "already served" doesn't show that order as clearly, and "was already serving" wrongly suggests he was still in the war when he joined the Knicks.

"Knives, horseshoes, wool tunics, and thousands of other artifacts" is the direct object of the verb "unearthed," and no punctuation should come between a verb and its object. A colon, comma, or dash would all wrongly separate them.

The introductory phrase "A government body officially known as the Althing" must describe the noun that comes right after the comma. Only choice B places "Iceland's parliament" there, which is the body called the Althing. The other choices make the phrase describe "the world's oldest parliaments," "the first meeting," or "930 CE," creating dangling modifiers.

The blank refers back to the two woodcuts, Evening at Carl Inn and Lake Basin in the High Sierra, so a plural pronoun and verb are needed: "they were." "It was" and "this was" are singular, and "some were" suggests only part of a group when both woodcuts are meant.

The first sentence ends after "an ethical AI-powered crowd-monitoring system." The rest, "Analyzing video streamed from cameras..., the AI algorithm determines crowd sizes...," is a full new sentence with its own subject and verb, so a period is needed. A comma, a dash, or no punctuation would leave two independent clauses joined improperly.

"However" here contrasts Scott-Heron's attitude with the journalists' praise in the previous sentence; it is an interrupting word inside a single sentence, so it needs commas on both sides. Choice D puts a semicolon before "however," which would leave "however, feeling that it didn't..." as a fragment with no main verb. A and B lack the needed comma after "however" or use a semicolon wrongly.

The subject, "Mary Madden of Ohio," is one person, and the time is the late 1800s, so the singular past-tense "was" is correct. "Are," "have been," and "were" are all plural forms that don't agree with a singular subject.

The sentence is a statement that contains an embedded question ("which link you should choose"), so it uses normal statement word order—subject before verb—and ends with a period. Inverted order ("should you choose") and a question mark belong only in direct questions.

The sentence describes a hypothetical past event: if the sugars had arrived long ago, they "could have reacted" with other molecules. That past hypothetical condition calls for the past perfect "had reached," which also matches "survived." Present ("reach," "are reaching") and future ("will reach") tenses don't fit an event in Earth's distant past.

"Which gave engravers control..." is a relative clause describing the Engravers' Copyright Act, and a comma correctly separates this extra information from the noun. A semicolon or period would cut off the "which" clause as a fragment, and no punctuation runs the name directly into the description.

There was one screw ("inserting a screw"), so the singular possessive "screw's" is needed, and it has many threads, which is simply plural, "threads," with no apostrophe. "Screws'" wrongly suggests several screws, and "thread's" or "threads'" wrongly make the threads possessive.

The photos belong to one photographer, Adams, so the singular possessive "photographer's" is needed. "Photos" is just plural and doesn't own anything, so it takes no apostrophe. The other choices either drop the possessive apostrophe or wrongly add one to "photos."

The opening phrase "Forming extensive networks via mycorrhizal association" must describe whoever forms those networks—the pine trees and the fungus. Only choice D puts "pine trees and the fungus Tricholoma matsutake" right after the phrase. The other choices make the phrase describe "it," "the transport of nutrients," or "nutrients," which creates a dangling modifier.

The text describes something that happens "each year" and uses the present tense ("starts," "journey"), so the present-tense "fly" is consistent. The past forms "flew," "were flying," and "had flown" don't fit a recurring, current event.

A colon after a complete clause ("a team... tried something new") correctly introduces an explanation of what that new thing was: "sequencing the DNA...." A semicolon or period would leave "sequencing the DNA..." as a fragment, and choice C puts the colon in the wrong spot, between "sequencing" and its object.

The blank refers to "the poems," which is plural, so the plural possessive pronoun "their" is correct. "Its" is singular, and "it's" and "they're" are contractions ("it is," "they are"), not possessives.

"By linking the Hudson River to Lake Erie" is an introductory phrase, so a comma should separate it from the main clause "the canal reduced transport time...." A semicolon or colon must follow a complete independent clause, which this phrase is not, and an opening parenthesis would never be closed.

"They were not the first in England to adopt the literary modes of classical antiquity" and "some of the most prominent figures... were also influenced..." are both independent clauses. "However" belongs to the second clause, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after it. Choices A and B use only commas, creating a comma splice, and C puts the semicolon after "however," attaching the transition to the wrong clause.

After the complete clause "Okie-Tex takes place in an area with low light pollution," the participle "ensuring" starts a phrase that describes the result of that location. Choices B and D add a new subject and verb after a comma, creating a comma splice, and C ("ensures") leaves a verb with no subject.

The subject is "Alexander's use," which is singular, so the singular verb "evokes" is required. The phrase "of 'we'" doesn't change the subject. "Are evoking," "have evoked," and "evoke" are plural forms.

Two independent clauses are joined here, so the correct punctuation is a comma followed by the conjunction "but." A comma alone (C) creates a comma splice, "but" without a comma (A) is a run-on, and a comma after "but" (B) is unnecessary.

"However" contrasts this sentence with the previous one (dozens of dances, but only five in competitions), so it is set off by a comma inside the sentence. The sentence then names the five dances, and a colon after a complete clause is the right way to introduce that list. A comma or semicolon after "however" can't introduce the list properly, and D's semicolon would leave the list as a fragment.

"Plant cell biologist" is a title that identifies Yuree Lee and is essential to the sentence, so no commas belong between the title and the name or between the name and the verb "showed." Choice B separates the subject from its verb, and A and D wrongly break up the title and name.

The sentence is in the past tense ("had drastically increased," "roamed"), describing events from Hawaiian history, so the simple past "ascended" fits. "By the time" with a past perfect main clause pairs with a simple past verb. The present and future forms don't match the time frame.
The subject "sound-based tools" is plural, so it needs the plural verb "enable." "Has enabled," "is enabling," and "enables" are all singular forms that don't agree with the subject.

The subject of the sentence is "The question," which is singular; everything from "of what cross-cultural traits" to "in the first place" just describes it. So the singular verb "animates" is needed. The plural nouns "traits," "modes," and "pressures" are tempting but aren't the subject, and "animating" isn't a complete verb.

The main verb of the sentence is "lent," so the blank must start a modifying phrase describing the result of that appeal: "earning her the moniker...." Using a finite verb like "earned," "had earned," or "earn" after the comma would attach a second verb with no conjunction, which is ungrammatical.

The interrupting phrase "assuming solar panel installers' cooperation" opens with a dash after "that," so it must close with a matching dash. Mixing a dash with a comma or colon (A, C) is incorrect, and leaving out punctuation (D) fails to close the interruption.

The opening phrase "Established in 1936 by African American novelist Richard Wright" must describe the noun right after the comma, and what Wright established was the South Side Writers Group. Choice A puts that group there, and "it" in the next clause then clearly refers to it. The other choices make the phrase describe "Chicago writers," "writers," or "Chicago," none of which Wright established in 1936.

The opening description—"laden with emojis and seemingly meaningless words"—describes the titles, so "the titles" must come right after the comma. Choices A, C, and D place "the listener," "each piece," or "the listener's approach" there instead, creating dangling modifiers.

"However" contrasts this sentence with the earlier point that the work relies on simulations; it interrupts a single clause, so it's set off by commas. What follows, "recommending evolving binary star systems...," is a participial phrase, not a clause, so a semicolon or period before or after "however" (A, C, D) would leave it as a fragment.

The subject is the single book, "A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields," so it needs a singular verb: "has enhanced." The phrase between commas describing the book doesn't change the subject, and the other choices are all plural forms.

"That is the oldest club for Black divers... and that has helped thousands..." is an essential clause describing the club, so no punctuation should separate "club" from "that." A comma or dash would wrongly split them, and "and" would connect the clause to nothing parallel.

After the complete clause about the collaboration, "showcasing the stylistic diversity..." is a participial phrase describing its result, and a comma correctly attaches it. Choice A creates a comma splice, while B and D turn the phrase into a separate fragment.

"It does not appear that the golden orb-weaver spider uses camouflage to capture its prey" and "the brightly colored arachnid seems to wait conspicuously..." are independent clauses. "Rather" introduces the second one, so a semicolon goes before it and a comma after. Commas alone (A, B) create a comma splice, and C attaches "rather" to the wrong clause.

"In 1919 Larrazolo was elected governor of New Mexico" and "in 1928 he became the nation's first Hispanic U.S. Senator" are both independent clauses, so they need a comma plus "and." A comma alone is a comma splice, and "and" without a comma or no punctuation runs them together.

The subject is "This hypothesis," and its main verb comes later: "cannot stand." The blank therefore must begin a phrase describing the hypothesis, so the participle "suggesting" is correct. Using a finite verb like "suggests" or "has suggested" would give the subject two main verbs with nothing joining them.

"Critic" is a title that directly identifies Stina Chyn and is needed to know who she is, so no commas go around her name. No comma is needed after "claims" either, since it introduces a quoted phrase that is part of the sentence's grammar. Each other choice adds at least one unneeded comma.

"The strings inside the instrument" is the subject and "are plucked" is its verb. No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, so no mark is needed after "instrument." A colon, dash, or comma would wrongly split them.

The text asks a direct question, which is then answered in the next sentences. Direct questions use question word order ("did the word 'chortle' come from") and end with a question mark. A uses a period, and B and D use statement word order.

"The measurement is based on how much and how quickly weight can be moved" and "one unit of mechanical horsepower is equivalent to..." are both independent clauses, and "for example" introduces the second one. So a semicolon goes before "for example" and a comma after. Commas alone (A, B) cause a comma splice, and D is a run-on.
"The use of Jamaican Creole" is the direct object of the verb "popularized," and no punctuation belongs between a verb and its object. A semicolon, comma, or colon would separate them incorrectly.

The pronoun refers back to "an object," a single specific thing already mentioned, so "it" is the clear and correct choice. "These" is plural, and "this" and "that" are less clear here because they could seem to refer to the sound rather than the object.

The sentence is a statement explaining a result ("which is why ganga has been used..."), not a question, so it uses subject-before-verb order and ends with a period. Choices C and D use question word order, and A wrongly adds a question mark.

The subject is "The Arrhenius equation," which is singular, so it needs the singular verb "remains." The phrase "named for its creator" just describes the equation. "Have remained," "remain," and "are remaining" are plural forms.

The subject is "The trailblazing accomplishments," which is plural, so the plural verb "attest" is correct. The singular name "Goldin" and the long description of her sit between the subject and verb but aren't the subject. "Attests," "has attested," and "is attesting" are singular.

The sentence needs a main verb for its subject, "the International Astronomical Union," and only "would finally acknowledge" supplies one. "To finally acknowledge," "having finally acknowledged," and "finally acknowledging" are not complete verbs, so they would leave the sentence a fragment.

The Dust Bowl happened in the 1930s, and the text uses the past tense ("was," "plagued," "reached"), so the simple past "affected" fits. Present ("are affecting") and future ("will affect," "will have affected") forms don't match a past event.

The main verb of the sentence is "shows," whose subject is "Aslanian's macroanalysis." The blank must begin a phrase describing the macroanalysis, so the participle "examining" is correct. A finite verb like "examines" or "had examined" would give the subject two verbs with nothing joining them; "examined" would wrongly suggest the analysis was examined.

After the colon, the text states the novel's central question directly, so it uses question word order ("will Umuofia's traditions be affected") and ends with a question mark. A and C use statement word order, and B ends a question with a period.

The opening phrase "A nearly frictionless (and... extremely slippery) state" renames superlubricity, so "superlubricity" must come right after the comma. Choice D does this. The other choices put "their COF," "two surfaces," or "reaching superlubricity" there, making the phrase describe the wrong thing.

The subject of the verb is "each one," which is singular, so the singular "is" is needed. The plural "couplets" and the long "while adhering..." phrase come between the subject and verb but don't change it. "Were," "have been," and "are" are plural forms.

"The innovative works of Congolese sculptor and architect Bodys Isek Kingelez" is the subject and "were featured" is its verb, so no punctuation should separate them. A semicolon, comma, or colon would split the subject from its verb.

The preposition "to" must be directly followed by its object, "the largest island of them all," so no punctuation belongs after it. The colon later in the sentence already introduces the island's name; a semicolon, dash, or comma after "to" would break up the phrase.

"Pioneering playwright" is a title that identifies Wakako Yamauchi, so no commas go between it and the name. The name is the subject of "compares," so no comma belongs after it either. Every other choice adds a comma that separates the title from the name or the subject from its verb.

The text explains how worker cooperatives generally work, using the present tense ("is," "stands," "are shared"), so the present-tense "benefit" fits. The past forms "benefited," "were benefiting," and "had benefited" don't match a general, ongoing description.

In standard English the verb "enable" takes an object followed by an infinitive: it enables someone "to" do something. So "enables cartographers... to create maps" is correct. "Create," "creating," and "created" don't fit that structure.

The writer asks a direct question ("What are atmospheric rivers, and how...") and then answers it, so the second half must also use question word order, "do they affect our weather," and end with a question mark. A ends a question with a period, and B and D use statement word order.

"Roughly 200,000 km²" describes the size of the Puntland Desert, and the whole phrase "the roughly 200,000 km² Puntland Desert" is the subject of "is classified." No commas should separate the measurement from the noun it describes or the subject from its verb, so no punctuation is needed. Each other choice adds a comma that breaks up the subject.

The pronoun refers to "a traditional violin," the single instrument whose curves Stradivari flattened, so the singular "it" is correct. "Those" and "them" are plural and would seem to point to the curves, and "one" doesn't clearly refer back to the violin.

The phrase "or FESTAC '77, as the event was more commonly known" interrupts the subject and is closed with a dash before "became," so it must open with a matching dash after "Culture." A colon or comma would not pair with the closing dash, and no punctuation would leave the interruption unopened.
The preposition "of" must be followed directly by its object, "all the elements on the periodic table," with no punctuation in between. A dash, comma, or colon would split the prepositional phrase.

The subject is "a unique tradition of embroidery," and its main verb is "remains," which comes later. The blank must start a phrase describing the tradition, so the participle "dating" is correct. A finite verb like "dates," "date," or "has dated" would give the subject two main verbs with nothing joining them.
The blank refers to the sculpture Mi Mama y Yo ("in its place"), so the singular possessive "its" is correct. "Their" is plural, and "it's" and "they're" are contractions, not possessives.
"Today" signals the present, so the present-tense "is" is correct: Paik is considered the first video artist now. "Was," "had been," and "will be" place the description in the past or future.

"Gitlin's use of the term referenced TV studios' practice of repackaging... as new content" and "in that era, even shows that varied only slightly... still attracted sizeable audiences" are both independent clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them, and the comma after "era" sets off the introductory phrase. The other choices join the two clauses with only a comma or nothing, creating a comma splice or run-on.
The subject "Such phrases" is plural, so it takes the plural verb "vary." The phrase "known as story starters" just describes the subject. "Has varied," "varies," and "is varying" are singular forms.
"Calida Garcia Rawles" is the subject and "was" is its verb, so no punctuation should come between them. A dash, colon, or comma would wrongly separate the subject from its verb.

"That" refers to "a writing technique," which is singular, so the verb must be singular: "creates." The present tense also fits a general definition. "Create," "are creating," and "have created" are plural forms.
The subject "ayllus" is plural, and the sentence describes the past Inca Empire, so the plural past-tense "were" is correct. "Is," "was," and "has been" are singular.

The first part is a complete clause ending with "two varieties of the sweet potato plant," and what follows names those two varieties. A colon is the right mark to introduce that explanation. A period or semicolon would leave the list of varieties as a fragment, and no punctuation runs them together awkwardly.

The subject is the single game, "Tracy Fullerton's Walden, a game," so it needs the singular verb "invites." The long description between commas, which mentions "writings" and "video games," doesn't change the subject. The other choices are plural forms.

The subject is "the shape," which is singular; "of each statue's ears" and "like the shape of each person's ears" only describe it. So the singular "is" is correct, and the present tense fits a fact that is still true. "Are," "were," and "have been" are plural.

The relative clause beginning with "which" needs a complete verb, and "provided" supplies one. "Having provided," "to provide," and "providing" are not complete verbs, so they would leave the "which" clause unfinished.

"Chile and Luxembourg" identifies exactly which fellow OECD nations are meant, so it is essential and takes no punctuation. A comma would treat the names as extra information and would need a closing comma, while a semicolon or colon can't come in the middle of this prepositional phrase.

The names "Thomas Hart Benton and Jackson Pollock" identify which artists are meant, so they are essential and take no commas, and no punctuation should separate the subject from "were featured." The other choices add a colon or commas that break up the subject or separate it from its verb.

The phrase "Upon recovering two years later" describes the person who recovered, Henry, so "Henry" must come right after it. Choice A does this. B and C make it seem that the reign recovered, and D starts with "it," so each creates a dangling modifier.
